title: Cabling Types: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Copper or fibre? One is cheap and short. The other is fast and goes far.

scenes.heading: Highway vs express lane
scenes.narration: Copper Ethernet is a multi lane highway. It's cheap and easy, but beyond a hundred metres the traffic gets congested, and the signal fades. Fibre is a dedicated express lane that uses light. It goes much further, and noise can't touch it. Multimode fibre is for shorter runs in a building. Single mode fibre is for long distances between sites.

scenes.heading: Distances to know
scenes.narration: A few distances show up on the exam. Copper stops at a hundred metres. Multimode gigabit fibre reaches five fifty metres. Single mode reaches five kilometres, or much more with better optics. And Cat six only carries ten gigabit to fifty-five metres, while Cat six A does a full hundred.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. Fibre has distance limits too, and they depend on the type. Not all Cat six carries ten gigabit for a hundred metres, only Cat six A. And a T D R test needs the interface shut down, because it sends test pulses down the cable.

items.right: Limits depend on the fibre type
Cat6 only to 55 m; Cat6a to 100 m

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Copper is cheap but stops at a hundred metres. Fibre goes further, and single mode goes furthest. Cat six A is what you need for ten gigabit at full distance. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva cabling lab.
